images.filename: Old Point Loma Lighthouse kitchen garden.png
images.caption:
A US National Park Ranger and a park volunteer tend the replica kitchen garden at the Old Point Loma Lighthouse. The garden features edible plants which might have been grown by residents of the lighthouse during its operation. Vegetables grown in this garden include root vegetables like carrots, herbs like sage and thyme, fruits like tomatoes and strawberries, and leafy greens like chard.
Workers were replacing signs that marked the vegetables grown. The ranger can be seen wearing a surgical mask due to federal regulations in place for the COVID-19 pandemic.

images.caption:
I visited San Diego last week with my family and one of the stops was the Old Point Loma Lighthouse in the Point Cabrillo National Monument.  This lighthouse was retired in 1891 as it was determined that it was situated too high to be useful.  When it was cloudy or foggy, the lighthouse was often ABOVE the fog or clouds and unable to be seen from the water.
When it was discontinued, the fresnel lens was removed.  Eventually it was turned into a museum and restored to how it appeared during the time it was in service.  It was re-equipped with the fresnel lens from the Miles Rock Lighthouse near San Francisco.  In addition, the assistant keeper’s quarters were turned into a nice museum of lighthouse technology.

The view from this spot is spectacular and if you have never visited here, it is totally worth the $5 charge to get into the area.

images.caption:
A tower of the House of Hospitality in Balboa Park, originally designed by Bertram Goodhue for the 1915 Panama-California Exposition. It is in the Spanish Colonial Revival architecture style, with highly ornamented Spanish Baroque detailing.   
Sometimes referred to it as Spanish Revival or Spanish Mission Style. Most of the Exposition structures were designed by en:Bertram Goodhue and en:Carleton Winslow, and built, for the Panama-California Exposition held in 1915.  The exposition commemorated the opening of the Panama Canal.
"According to what I have read, it is actually a unique style of architecture that combines elements of some of the great structures found in Spain, as well as influences from some of the beautiful cathedrals found in Mexico.
